subject: Art & Design
title: Sustainable Fashion: The Industry's Reckoning
description: A 60-second lesson on Sustainable Fashion: The Industry's Reckoning.

hook.text: 92 million tons of textile waste are produced every year.

buildup.text: Sustainable fashion aims to reduce environmental impact through ethical sourcing, slow production, and circular design.

discovery.text: Circular fashion designs clothes to be repaired, resold, or recycled.

twist.text: Many brands 'greenwash' — claiming sustainability while barely changing practices.

climax.text: Stella McCartney, Eileen Fisher, and Reformation prove luxury and sustainability can coexist.

punchline.text: Sustainable fashion isn't a trend. It's a survival requirement for the industry.

quiz.question: What is 'greenwashing' in the fashion industry?
options: Brands falsely claiming sustainability while barely changing practices
Dyeing all fabrics green for eco-branding
A washing technique that reduces water usage

details.summary: The fashion industry faces an environmental crisis: it consumes 93 billion cubic meters of water annually, generates 20% of global wastewater, and is the second-largest industrial polluter.
details.whyItMatters: Fashion's environmental impact is staggering and unsustainable. The industry must transform or face regulation, consumer backlash, and resource depletion that threaten its own survival.
takeaways: Fashion is the second-largest industrial polluter globally
The industry consumes 93 billion cubic meters of water yearly
Circular design and recycled materials offer partial solutions

faq.question: What is circular fashion?
faq.answer: Circular fashion designs garments for longevity, repair, and eventual recycling rather than disposal. Brands take back old garments, recycle fibers into new fabric, and design for disassembly.

faq.question: Is greenwashing a problem in sustainable fashion?
faq.answer: Enormously. Many brands market 'sustainable' collections that represent less than 1% of their production while continuing business as usual. Terms like 'eco-friendly' and 'conscious' are unregulated. True sustainability requires systemic change, not small capsule collections.
